1352.title: Shakuntala
1352.hook: a ring slips into a river, and a king forgets: the poet Kalidasa tells Shakuntala's story his own way
1352.howItsDone: Shakuntala's story is told in the Mahabharata's first book, and Kalidasa's play retells it with the ring and the curse; the play is still read, staged and danced in India and beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakuntala in the king's hall, holding her son's hand and telling a king who claimed not to know her the truth about himself.

A ring slips off a woman's finger at a sacred pool, and sinks. She doesn't notice. Later a fisherman cuts open a fish, finds a royal ring inside, and is arrested as a thief. That ring isn't in the Mahabharata at all. It belongs to a play, Shakuntala, by the poet Kalidasa, who took the epic's story and told it his own way. On our last day with her, the two tellings sit side by side, and then we meet the boy she brought to court.
screen: `A RING SINKS IN A RIVER.` → `A FISHERMAN, A FISH, A KING.` → `TWO TELLINGS, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Start with the epic. Shakuntala tells the king the truth, and a voice from the sky backs her. Then comes a line that's easy to skip, in paraphrase: the king says he knew her all along, but wanted his people to hear it from heaven, so no one would doubt the child. In the epic, the forgetting is a choice, and her words carry the scene. Now the play. Kalidasa adds a sage with a short temper, Durvasa. He arrives at the hermitage while Shakuntala sits lost in thoughts of her husband, and she doesn't greet him. So he curses her: the one you're thinking of will forget you. A friend begs for mercy, and the curse is softened: a token will bring the memory back. The token is the ring, and the ring is in the water. So in the play the king's forgetting is a curse, not a choice. When the fisherman's ring reaches him, it all comes flooding back, and he grieves. Readers have argued over the change. Some say it makes the king easier to forgive. Some say it takes the scene away from her voice. Both tellings end with the boy. In the play, the king finds him in a heavenly hermitage, prying open a lion cub's mouth to count its teeth. In the epic, the boy is named Bharata, and the royal line takes its name from him. Tradition hears his name in Bharat, one of India's own names for itself, though other stories lay claim to that name too.
screen: `IN THE EPIC, THE KING CHOOSES TO FORGET` · `IN THE PLAY, A SAGE'S CURSE` · `THE RING IN THE FISH` · `A BOY NAMED BHARATA`

Let it bring the person back the way the ring did for the king, their face, their voice, one ordinary moment, without pushing for a big feeling. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer.

1353.title: Andal
1353.hook: an offering meant for the gods, and a jackal from the forest sniffing at it: Andal's picture of the marriage she refused
1353.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnava Hindus honor Andal as one of the Alvars; her Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumoli are recited in temples and homes, and her shrine at Srivilliputtur is a place of pilgrimage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakuntala told twice: a king who chooses to forget, and a king cursed to forget until a ring comes back in a fish. Today, a poet who speaks for herself.

An offering is laid out for the gods. Priests have prepared it with care, by the rules, for the sacred fire. Then a jackal slips in from the forest and sniffs at it. Ruined. Nobody could offer it now. That rough little picture comes from a young woman's poem, and she's using it about herself: what would happen to her if anyone so much as talked of marrying her to a man. The woman is Andal, and today she speaks for herself.
screen: `AN OFFERING FOR THE GODS.` → `A JACKAL FROM THE FOREST.` → `ANDAL SPEAKS FOR HERSELF.`

segments.voice: Year three met Andal at dawn, in the Tiruppavai, waking her friends for the dawn vow, and with the garland she tried on before her father carried it to the temple. That's Andal in a group, one cowherd girl among many. Her other work, the Nachiyar Tirumoli, the sacred words of the lady, sounds different. Here she's mostly alone, and the voice is hers. Take the jackal verse, in paraphrase. My heart is set on the Lord who holds the conch and the wheel. If anyone speaks of giving me to a mortal man, I won't live. It would be like the offering made for the gods being sniffed by a jackal of the forest. She doesn't say marriage is bad. She says she is already set apart, already promised, and anything else would spoil the offering. Now notice whom she asks for help. The same book opens with her pleading with Kama, the god of desire, sweeping the ground and drawing in the sand for him, asking him to join her to the Lord. She asks the very god of ordinary love to lead her away from an ordinary match. Two readings sit side by side. Sri Vaishnava teachers read her longing as the soul's longing for God, the way a devotee stands before the Lord. Other readers also hear a young woman saying in her own words whom she will and won't belong to. The tradition never had to pick one. It counts her among the Alvars, the poet-saints, and keeps singing her verses.
screen: `HER OTHER BOOK, IN HER OWN VOICE` · `THE OFFERING AND THE JACKAL` · `ASKING THE GOD OF DESIRE FOR HELP` · `THE SOUL'S LONGING, A GIRL'S CHOICE`

1354.title: Andal
1354.hook: Andal questions a conch shell: does his mouth smell of camphor, or of the lotus?
1354.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnava Hindus recite Andal's Nachiyar Tirumoli in temples and homes, and in Vishnu worship the conch is blown and held as one of the Lord's own emblems.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Andal and the offering a jackal sniffed: her picture of any match but the Lord.

Does it smell of camphor? Of the lotus? Is it sweet? A young woman is asking, urgently, and she's asking a seashell. Not any shell: the white conch that rests in the hand of Vishnu, and that Krishna lifts to his lips and blows. She wants to know what his mouth is like, and the conch is the only one who'd know. It's Andal again, in the seventh song of the Nachiyar Tirumoli, and she's jealous of a shell.
screen: `CAMPHOR? THE LOTUS? IS IT SWEET?` → `THE WHITE CONCH.` → `JEALOUS OF A SHELL.`

segments.voice: The opening, in paraphrase: does it smell of camphor, of the lotus, does his coral mouth taste sweet? I long to know. Tell me, white conch of the deep sea, what is the scent and taste of the lips of the one who broke the elephant's tusk? Then the questions turn into complaints. You were born in the ocean, she tells the conch, and now you live in his hand. You rest on his mouth while the rest of us wait. Others can only stand and look at him from afar, and you, a shell, go right up to his lips. It's a love poem, and a funny one: she's talking to an object, and envying it. So why a conch? In the Bhagavad Gita, before the battle, Krishna blows his conch, named Panchajanya. For a Vaishnava listener, the conch in the poem isn't decoration. It's one of the Lord's own emblems, held in his hand, carrying his breath. There's a second layer. Sri Vaishnava teachers read the conch as a picture of the devotee the Lord keeps nearest, close enough to carry his breath. So Andal's envy is also a wish: let me be that close, let my life be the instrument his breath moves through. And a third. This is temple scripture, recited by priests and families, full of taste and scent and lips and jealousy. The tradition didn't clean it up. It kept a young woman's desire, plain and bodily, as a way of talking about God.
screen: `QUESTIONS FOR A SEASHELL` · `ENVY OF THE ONE AT HIS LIPS` · `THE CONCH IN KRISHNA'S HAND` · `DESIRE KEPT AS SCRIPTURE`

1355.title: Andal
1355.hook: Andal tells a friend her dream: a wedding, step by step, with the Lord as the groom
1355.howItsDone: Some Sri Vaishnava families sing Andal's Varanam Ayiram at weddings, and celebrate her marriage to the Lord at her temple in Srivilliputtur and at Srirangam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Andal and the white conch: camphor or lotus, and a young woman jealous of a shell.

Friend, I had a dream. That's roughly how the song begins, and what follows is a wedding. Elephants first, a thousand of them, the song says, circling round as the groom comes into town. Then the canopy, the drums, the bride's hand taken, the walk around the fire. Every detail is there, the way you'd tell your closest friend the morning after a dream you can't shake. The dreamer is Andal, and the groom is the Lord. Our last day with her: the dream, and the ending tradition gives her.
screen: `FRIEND, I HAD A DREAM.` → `ELEPHANTS, DRUMS, A CANOPY.` → `THE DREAM, AND THE ENDING.`

segments.voice: The song is the sixth in the Nachiyar Tirumoli, named for its opening words, Varanam Ayiram, a thousand elephants. In paraphrase, each verse is one moment of the wedding, and each closes with something like, I dreamed it, friend. The town is decorated. A pavilion goes up, hung with pearls. The groom arrives. The relatives gather; the bride is dressed. He takes her hand. They walk around the sacred fire together. He sets her foot on the grinding stone, one of the steps of the rite. It's a full Tamil wedding, told from the inside, by a bride who hasn't had one. In the last two days she refused a mortal husband and envied a shell. Here, at last, she lets herself have the whole thing, in a dream. And some Sri Vaishnava families sing Varanam Ayiram at their own weddings, so a young woman's dream of marrying God becomes the song that blesses ordinary couples. Then the ending, as tradition tells it. Her father, Periyalvar, worries: whom can she marry? The story says the Lord of the temple at Srirangam lets it be known that he will take her. So her father brings her there, dressed as a bride. She walks into the shrine, toward the reclining image of the Lord, and she isn't seen again. Tradition says she became one with him. The texts are her songs; the ending is the story her community tells. Andal's poems don't describe it. In them, the wedding stays a dream.
screen: `A THOUSAND ELEPHANTS` · `THE WEDDING, STEP BY STEP` · `SUNG AGAIN AT WEDDINGS` · `THE BRIDE WHO WALKED INTO THE SHRINE`

1356.title: Mirabai
1356.hook: a princess ties bells to her ankles and dances in public, and people call her mad
1356.howItsDone: Mira's songs are sung as bhajans, with drums and cymbals, in temples, homes and concert halls, and some are danced in classical and folk styles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Andal's dream of a wedding: a thousand elephants, and a bride who walked into the shrine. Today, a princess with bells on her feet.

Small brass bells, strung on a cord and tied around the ankles. Every step rings. You can't sneak anywhere wearing them; that's rather the point. Dancers wear them on stage. In one of the songs sung in her name, a princess ties them on and dances, in public, for Krishna. The town talks. Her husband's family is mortified. And the song hides none of it. It repeats what people said about her, and then it shrugs. Year three heard Mira's poison cup and her treasure. Today, her feet.
screen: `BELLS TIED AROUND THE ANKLES.` → `THE TOWN TALKS.` → `TODAY, HER FEET.`

segments.voice: The song opens with the line people know it by, pag ghunghroo bandh Mira nachi re. The sense, in paraphrase: Mira tied bells on her feet and danced. I've made myself my Lord's own servant. People say Mira's gone mad. My mother-in-law says I've ruined the family. And the last line: Mira's Lord is Giridhar, and she has met the undying one with ease. First, who's speaking about her. The people, the mother-in-law, the family: the song lets them all have their say. It doesn't argue back. It just goes on dancing. The mother-in-law's word, ruin of the family, shows the line a royal woman crossed by dancing in the open, and the song names it. Second, the word for mad there is bawari, and in Mira's songs madness isn't only an insult. In another song she calls herself prem diwani, mad with love. So the charge the town throws at her becomes something she wears, like the bells. Third, the bells make devotion something you can hear. Bhakti, the way of loving devotion, isn't only a feeling in the chest. In Mira's songs it moves the feet, keeps a rhythm, gathers a crowd. These songs are still sung with a drum and cymbals, in temples and living rooms, and sometimes danced. A song about a woman who wouldn't keep still is very hard to sing sitting still.
screen: `MIRA TIED BELLS ON HER FEET` · `THE TOWN HAS ITS SAY` · `MAD, THE WORD SHE WEARS` · `DEVOTION YOU CAN HEAR`

1357.title: Mirabai
1357.hook: a holy man in Vrindavan won't meet a woman, and Mira sends him one sentence
1357.howItsDone: Vrindavan remains a place of pilgrimage for Krishna devotees, and stories of Mira's time there are told alongside her songs in bhajan gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai with bells on her ankles, dancing while the town called her mad, and wearing the word as her own.

A door, and a message passed through it. On one side, a learned renunciant in Vrindavan who has made a rule for himself: he doesn't meet women. On the other, a woman who has walked a long way to see him, and has just been turned away. She doesn't argue about the rule. She sends back a single sentence, and by the end of the story, the door opens. The woman is Mira, and the sentence is today's whole lesson.
screen: `A DOOR, AND A MESSAGE.` → `A RULE: NO WOMEN.` → `ONE SENTENCE BACK.`

segments.voice: First, where she is. Tradition says that after the troubles with her husband's family, Mira left the palace and took to the road, and came to Vrindavan, the country of Krishna's childhood, where the cowherd girls, the gopis, once ran to the sound of his flute. Holy people and teachers lived there. The story names one of them as Jiva Goswami, a scholar of Krishna devotion; some tellings name another teacher. The story, in paraphrase: Mira asks to meet him. Word comes back that he has vowed not to see women. And Mira answers, roughly: I thought there was only one man in Vrindavan, Krishna. I didn't know anyone else here was claiming to be a man. The renunciant hears it, and comes out to meet her. It's sharp, and it's funny. But under the wit is a teaching that belongs to Vrindavan itself. In the devotion Vrindavan is known for, the soul stands before Krishna the way the gopis did: as the beloved, waiting for him. Before him, no one is the man of the house. So the rule that kept her out rested on a difference that, in that place, she says doesn't count. And she doesn't attack his vow, or his learning, or him. She takes the faith of the place more seriously than the rule does, and lets that speak. Last, this isn't a record anyone wrote down at the door. It's one of the stories told about her, remembered because it teaches, the way a parable does.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai at a closed door in Vrindavan, answering that there was only one man there.

This week, three women's voices. Shakuntala, told twice, in an epic and in a play. Andal refusing a mortal groom, questioning a conch, dreaming her wedding. And Mira, dancing in bells and talking her way through a closed door. What reaches us of each one has been carried, retold, sung, by people who loved them. Mira's songs show it plainly, because they end with a signature. To close the week, the last line of a Mira song.
screen: `THREE WOMEN'S VOICES THIS WEEK.` → `CARRIED BY PEOPLE WHO LOVED THEM.` → `THE LAST LINE OF A SONG.`

segments.voice: Listen to how a Mira song ends. Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar. Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the clever one who lifted the mountain. The phrase comes back at the close of song after song sung in her name, like a seal pressed into wax. Singers call that kind of closing name a chhap, a stamp. It tells you whose song it is. Now, how do these songs reach us? By being sung: wandering singers, temple gatherings, women singing at home, families passing down the words they knew. And as they're sung, the same song can turn up in different words in different places. So when a song ends with Mira's stamp, what it promises is a voice and a lineage, not a notarized author. That raises an honest question the songs can't settle: which lines go back to Mira's own lips? Some readers sort the songs into older and newer. Others say the question misses the point, since a song stays alive by being sung, changing a little in every mouth. Both views take her seriously. Last, the stamp does something gentle. Whoever sings it, wherever, ends by stepping aside: not my Lord, but Mira's Lord. Each singer lends Mira their voice for a few minutes, and Mira lends them her love. That's how a woman who, tradition says, left a palace with almost nothing is still being sung.
